name: Ashkenazi

database_scope.purpose: Sourced reference for Ashkenazi minhagim and halachic practice. It records what the cited sources say, with a confidence level for each entry, and is not a psak.
database_scope.coverage_note: 26 sourced topics and 5 distinctive customs, compiled from the cited sources in October 2026. Each entry carries a confidence level (well-attested, disputed, regional, needs-review). 20 topics have no community-specific source and are listed under 'gaps' rather than filled with generic text.

identity.primary_origin: Medieval Germany and the Rhineland, later Poland, Lithuania and the rest of Eastern Europe
secondary_centers: Frankfurt and the German communities (Minhag Ashkenaz proper)
Hasidic courts such as Chabad-Lubavitch, Satmar, Belz and Ger
Washington Heights, New York (Kehal Adas Yeshurun)

subgroups.name: Hasidic (Nusach Sefard / Nusach Ari)
subgroups.note: Courts including Chabad-Lubavitch, Satmar, Belz, Ger, Vizhnitz, Bobov, Breslov, Munkacs and Skver. They pray Nusach Sefard, a Polish Ashkenazi base with Lurianic changes; Chabad uses its own Nusach Ari siddur compiled by R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi. Many customs follow the Ari and the Zohar rather than the Rema.

subgroups.name: Litvish / Yeshivish
subgroups.note: Nusach Ashkenaz (Minhag Polin), shaped heavily by the Vilna Gaon (Gra) and, in Israel, by the Gra's disciples. The Mishnah Berurah is the dominant practical code.

subgroups.name: German / Yekke (Minhag Ashkenaz proper)
subgroups.note: Western Ashkenazi rite of Frankfurt and the German communities, preserved by Kehal Adas Yeshurun (Washington Heights) and documented by Machon Moreshes Ashkenaz (R. Binyomin Shlomo Hamburger, Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz).

subgroups.name: Modern Orthodox
subgroups.note: Mostly Nusach Ashkenaz, often following rulings of Rav Joseph B. Soloveitchik and Rav Moshe Feinstein. Where a Soloveitchik position is cited here, it is recorded as such.

subgroups.name: Liturgical axis: Nusach Ashkenaz vs Nusach Sefard
subgroups.note: Cuts across the subgroups. Nusach Ashkenaz: Litvish, Yekke, most Modern Orthodox. Nusach Sefard / Ari: Hasidim and Jews of Hasidic descent.

timeline.event: R. Eleazar of Worms (Rokeach) records a chain of transmission of the Ashkenazi prayer text from the Kalonymide family of Mainz and Speyer.
timeline.halachic_impact: Grounds the principle that the Ashkenazi liturgical text may not be altered; cited in Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz (Peirushei Siddur HaTefillah LaRokeach vol. 1 p. 229).

timeline.event: The Rosh, having fled Germany for Toledo, writes that he follows the tradition of the sages of Ashkenaz rather than local Sephardic tradition (Shu't HaRosh 20:20).
timeline.halachic_impact: Classic precedent for adhering to Ashkenazi ancestral custom.

timeline.event: The Tur (OC 583) records that in Germany a sweet apple is eaten with honey on Rosh Hashana.
timeline.halachic_impact: Origin of the Ashkenazi simanim custom later codified by the Rema.

timeline.event: Shulchan Aruch published; the Rema adds glosses recording the custom of Ashkenaz/Poland.
timeline.halachic_impact: The Rema becomes the baseline authority for all Ashkenazi subgroups.

timeline.event: The Ari (R. Yitzchak Luria) in Safed; his customs and prayer arrangements later spread to Eastern Europe.
timeline.halachic_impact: Basis of Nusach Sefard / Nusach Ari and of many Hasidic customs (Omer mourning, upsherin, tefillin on Chol HaMoed).

timeline.event: Rise of Hasidism; R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi compiles his siddur 'al pi nusach ha-Ari'; avoiding gebrokts gains prominence.
timeline.halachic_impact: Creates the Nusach Ashkenaz vs Sefard axis and Hasidic Pesach stringencies.

timeline.event: Chatam Sofer (Shu't OC 16) defends Nusach Ashkenaz against the Hasidic switch to Nusach Sefard.
timeline.halachic_impact: Hungarian/German (Oberlander) communities keep Nusach Ashkenaz and related customs.

timeline.event: R. Nachman of Breslov dies in Uman (1810); R. Nosson organizes the first Rosh Hashana gathering at his grave (1811).
timeline.halachic_impact: Origin of the Breslov Rosh Hashana kibbutz in Uman.

timeline.event: Destruction of German and East European Jewry; German refugees found communities such as Kehal Adas Yeshurun, New York.
timeline.halachic_impact: Rav Shimon Schwab frames KAJ as heir to the 'thousand year old sacred minhag Ashkenaz' (quoted in Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz).

timeline.event: R. Binyomin Shlomo Hamburger founds Machon Moreshes Ashkenaz and publishes Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz.
timeline.halachic_impact: Revives documented German custom; vol. 5 (5778) devoted to tefillin on Chol HaMoed.

primary_codes: Shulchan Aruch (R. Yosef Karo, 1563) with the glosses (Mappah) of R. Moshe Isserles (Rema, d. 1572)
later_poskim: R. Joseph B. Soloveitchik (as recorded in Nefesh HaRav)
core_halachic_authorities.decision_principle: Where the Rema records Ashkenazi custom against the Shulchan Aruch, Ashkenazim follow the Rema. Later authorities (Magen Avraham, Mishnah Berurah, Aruch HaShulchan) refine that practice. Hasidic communities often switch to Lurianic/Zoharic practice instead, and followers of the Gra to his rulings. Ancestral custom (minhag avot) is treated as binding, as Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz stresses.

runtime.practice_baseline: Practice rests on the Shulchan Aruch as glossed by the Rema and refined by the Magen Avraham, Taz, Mishnah Berurah and Aruch HaShulchan, with Hasidic courts adding Lurianic customs and their own minhag books, and German communities following Minhag Ashkenaz.

halacha_index.topic: Nusach: Ashkenaz vs Sefard vs Ari
halacha_index.summary: Nusach Ashkenaz recites Baruch She'amar before Hodu; Nusach Sefard, used by Hasidim, follows the Ari in reciting Hodu before Baruch She'amar and adds 've-yatzmach purkanei vi-karev meshichei' in Kaddish. Chabad uses its own Nusach Ari siddur compiled by R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi.
common_practices: Each family keeps its ancestral nusach
Hasidic courts daven Nusach Sefard; Chabad daven Nusach Ari (Siddur Tehillat Hashem)

variants.practice: Nusach Ashkenaz (Minhag Polin): Baruch She'amar precedes Hodu.
variants.source: 18Forty, 'The Siddur Has a Lot of Prayers. Where Did They Come From?'

variants.practice: Nusach Sefard: Hodu before Baruch She'amar; 've-yatzmach purkanei' in Kaddish.
variants.source: 18Forty, 'The Siddur Has a Lot of Prayers'

variants.practice: Nusach Ari as compiled by R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, a distinct version, not identical with general Nusach Sefard.
variants.source: 18Forty, ibid.; Yeshiva.co Ask the Rabbi #753

variants.subgroup: German / Yekke and Chatam Sofer communities
variants.practice: Minhag Ashkenaz proper. The Chatam Sofer argued that Rashi, the Tosafists, Maharam of Rothenburg, the Rosh and the Tur all prayed Nusach Ashkenaz.
variants.source: Shu't Chatam Sofer OC 16, quoted in Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz (English synopsis), Introduction p. 14

halacha_index.source: Shu't Chatam Sofer, Orach Chaim 16 (as quoted in R. B. S. Hamburger, Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz: Synopsis of Volumes I-IV, Machon Moreshes Ashkenaz 2010, p. 14)
halacha_index.review_notes: Exact textual differences between individual Hasidic court siddurim are not documented here.

references.title: The Siddur Has a Lot of Prayers. Where Did They Come From? - 18Forty

halacha_index.summary_he: נוסח אשכנז אומר "ברוך שאמר" לפני "הודו". נוסח ספרד, שבו משתמשים החסידים, הולך אחרי האר"י ואומר "הודו" לפני "ברוך שאמר", ומוסיף בקדיש "ויצמח פורקניה ויקרב משיחיה". חב"ד משתמשת בסידור נוסח האר"י משלה, שערך רבי שניאור זלמן מליאדי.

halacha_index.summary: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz documents the following German customs as distinct chapters: a distinct pronunciation of the cholam, praying at a slow pace, waiting for the community leader to finish his Amidah, introducing Shema with 'Kel Melech Ne'eman', reading Shema aloud and with cantillation, omitting 'Go'alenu Hashem Tzevakot Shemo' before the morning Amidah, the congregation remaining silent during the chazzan's Kedusha, the chazzan wearing a tallit, omitting Berikh Shemei when the Torah is taken out, and reading the haftara from a scroll.
common_practices: Slow, measured tefillah
Chazzan wears tallit at every service
Berikh Shemei omitted

variants.practice: As listed in the summary.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, table of contents, pp. 21-101

halacha_index.source: R. Binyomin Shlomo Hamburger, Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz: Minhag Ashkenaz Sources and Roots, Synopsis of Volumes I-IV (Bnei Brak 2010), table of contents
halacha_index.review_notes: Only the table of contents and introduction were read; the specifics of each chapter (e.g. exact cholam sound) were not opened.
halacha_index.topic_he: מנהגי בתי הכנסת של יהדות גרמניה (יקים)
halacha_index.summary_he: הספר "שורשי מנהג אשכנז" מתעד מנהגים גרמניים אלה כפרקים נפרדים: הגייה מיוחדת של החולם, תפילה בקצב איטי, המתנה לראש הקהילה עד שיסיים את עמידתו, פתיחת קריאת שמע ב"אל מלך נאמן", קריאת שמע בקול רם ובטעמי המקרא, השמטת "גואלנו ה' צבאות שמו" לפני עמידת שחרית, שתיקת הקהל בקדושה של החזן, חזן הלובש טלית, השמטת "בריך שמיה" בהוצאת ספר התורה, וקריאת ההפטרה מתוך מגילה.

halacha_index.summary: The Shulchan Aruch (OC 31:2) forbids wearing tefillin on Chol HaMoed. The Rema records that the custom 'in all these regions' is to wear them with a beracha, said quietly in shul. Today practice splits sharply by subgroup.
common_practices: Those who wear them remove them before Hallel
Do not mix customs within one minyan (Mishnah Berurah 31:8)

variants.practice: Wear with a beracha, recited quietly.
variants.source: Rema OC 31:2; Divrei Kehillos p. 329 as cited on KAYJ forum; Aish.com 'Tefillin on Chol HaMoed'

variants.practice: Wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed.
variants.source: Minhagei Chasam Sofer 8:7, as cited by shulchanaruchharav.com 'Tefillin on Chol Hamoed'

variants.subgroup: Eastern European Ashkenazim who wear them
variants.practice: Many wear without a beracha, following the Taz.
variants.source: Taz OC 31:2, cited by R. Chaim Jachter, Kol Torah; Aruch HaShulchan OC 31:4 as summarized by Mekoros

variants.practice: Do not wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed, following the Zohar.
variants.source: shulchanaruchharav.com 'Tefillin on Chol Hamoed': 'The Sefaradi and general Chassidic custom is not to put on Tefillin at all during Chol Hamoed'

variants.practice: Do not wear; Rav Chaim Soloveitchik did not wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed.
variants.source: Biur HaGra OC 31:2; R. Chaim Jachter, Kol Torah, 'Tefillin on Chol Hamoed'

variants.practice: Public custom is not to wear; those with a diaspora custom may wear privately.
variants.source: R. Chaim Jachter, Kol Torah; Halachipedia 'Tefillin on Chol HaMoed'

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Aruch and Rema, Orach Chaim 31:2; Mishnah Berurah 31:8; Igrot Moshe OC 5 (as cited)
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Moshe Feinstein permits keeping one's custom even in a minyan with the other practice, as reported by JewishPress. Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz vol. 5 is entirely devoted to this question.

halacha_index.summary_he: השולחן ערוך (או"ח לא:ב) אוסר להניח תפילין בחול המועד. הרמ"א מביא שהמנהג "בכל המדינות האלה" הוא להניחן בברכה, שנאמרת בלחש בבית הכנסת. כיום המנהג נחלק בחדות לפי עדות המשנה.

halacha_index.summary: In German custom boys and unmarried men wear a tallit at prayer. In most East European communities a tallit is worn only after marriage.

variants.practice: Boys begin wearing a tallit from a young age; R. Yechiel Michel Schlesinger wore a tallit while still unmarried at the Mir 'in accordance with the German custom'.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, Introduction p. 11; Chabad.org '15 Facts About Yekkes'

halacha_index.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, Introduction p. 11 (citing Eish Tamid, Jerusalem 1989, p. 826)
halacha_index.review_notes: The East European post-marriage custom is implied by the anecdote but not independently sourced here.
halacha_index.summary_he: במנהג גרמניה בחורים ורווקים עוטים טלית בתפילה. ברוב קהילות מזרח אירופה עוטים טלית רק אחרי הנישואין.

halacha_index.summary: Candles are lit before sunset, at a fixed offset set by local custom.
common_practices: 18 minutes before sunset, which R. Ari Enkin (OU Torah, 'Candle Lighting Time') calls 'the most widespread' custom

variants.practice: 18 minutes before sunset.
variants.source: OU Torah, Halacha L'Maaseh, 'Shabbat Candles'

variants.practice: 40 minutes before sunset; R. Ari Enkin derives it from 'a view which requires one to add half of a halachic hour to one's Shabbat', which reaches forty minutes at the height of summer.
variants.source: OU Torah, Halacha L'Maaseh; Aish.com citing Minchas Yitzchak 9:20, Sefer Eretz Yisrael p. 26, Badei HaShulchan 73:14

variants.subgroup: Satmar; Boro Park luach; UK calendars
variants.practice: 15 minutes before sunset.
variants.source: R. Ari Enkin, Dalet Amot of Halacha, citing Machzor Divrei Yoel and Zemirot Divrei Yoel

halacha_index.source: OU Torah, 'Candle Lighting Time' (Dalet Amot of Halacha) and 'Shabbat Candles' (Halacha L'Maaseh)
halacha_index.review_notes: The 18-minute figure has no single clear origin, as Enkin notes. Enkin states that 'all calendars in the UK as well as the official Boro Park luach' list 15 minutes, but he does not name which Boro Park luach he means.
halacha_index.summary_he: מדליקים נרות לפני השקיעה, במרווח קבוע שנקבע לפי המנהג המקומי.

halacha_index.summary: In German custom the hands are washed for bread before Kiddush on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and the bread is broken immediately after the Kiddush wine. Other Ashkenazim make Kiddush first and then wash.
common_practices: Kiddush, then washing (non-German Ashkenazim)

variants.practice: Wash before Kiddush.
variants.source: Rema OC 271:12 (custom not to be changed), as cited in JewishPress 'Washing Before Kiddush: Just For Yekkes?'; Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz vol. 2 pp. 258ff; synopsis chapter 'Performing Netilat Yadayim Before Kiddush' p. 77

halacha_index.source: Rema, Orach Chaim 271:12; Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz vol. 2 p. 258ff
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Yaakov Hoffman (JewishPress, 2019) calls washing before Kiddush 'widespread (though not universal) among medieval Jewry – both Sefardic and Ashkenazic'. He writes that from about the 16th century the custom of washing after Kiddush gained popularity, tracing the shift to Taz 271:14 and the Biur HaGra.

halacha_index.summary_he: במנהג גרמניה נוטלים ידיים לסעודה לפני הקידוש בשבת וביום טוב, ובוצעים את הלחם מיד אחרי יין הקידוש. אשכנזים אחרים מקדשים תחילה ואחר כך נוטלים ידיים.

halacha_index.summary: A sweet apple is dipped in honey at the start of the meal with the prayer for a sweet year. Nuts are avoided because the gematria of 'egoz' equals 'chet' (sin).
common_practices: Apple in honey after hamotzi, with borei pri ha-etz and yehi ratzon
Avoid nuts
halacha_index.source: Tur, Orach Chaim 583:1; Rema, Orach Chaim 583:1-2; Darkhei Moshe OC 583:3
halacha_index.review_notes: The Tur attributes the apple-and-honey custom specifically to Germany. Additional simanim (fish, head) are cited in Shulchan Aruch HaRav 583:2 per dinonline.

references.title: The Rosh Hashanah Simanim: Their Sources and Meaning

halacha_index.summary_he: בתחילת הסעודה טובלים תפוח מתוק בדבש ואומרים תפילה לשנה מתוקה. נמנעים מאגוזים, כי גימטריית "אגוז" כגימטריית "חטא".

halacha_index.summary: Breslov Hasidim travel to the grave of R. Nachman in Uman for Rosh Hashana, based on R. Nachman's statement 'my entire mission is Rosh Hashanah' and R. Nosson's organization of the gathering from 1811.

variants.practice: Rosh Hashana kibbutz at the tziyun in Uman.
variants.source: Breslov Research Institute, 'The Road to Uman #1' (breslov.org)

halacha_index.source: Breslov.org, 'The Road to Uman # 1' (translation commissioned by Breslov Research Institute for 'Uman, Uman, Rosh Hashanah')
halacha_index.review_notes: Primary Breslov texts (Chayei Moharan, Yemei Moharnat) were not opened directly.
halacha_index.summary_he: חסידי ברסלב נוסעים לציון רבי נחמן באומן לראש השנה, על פי דברי רבי נחמן "כל עיקר שלי הוא ראש השנה" ועל פי ארגון ההתכנסות בידי רבי נתן משנת 1811.

halacha_index.topic: Eating in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret (diaspora)
halacha_index.summary: The Shulchan Aruch (OC 668:1) rules that in the diaspora one eats in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret without the beracha. Customs vary widely.
common_practices: No 'leishev ba-sukkah' beracha
Not sleeping in the sukkah (Mishnah Berurah 668:6)

variants.practice: All meals in the sukkah, without the beracha.
variants.source: Shulchan Aruch OC 668:1; etzion.org.il 'Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah (2)'

variants.practice: Kiddush and all eating and drinking, even water, in the sukkah by night and day; not sleeping there; no Yehi Ratzon on leaving the sukkah.
variants.source: Chabad.org 'A Deeper Look at Shemini Atzeret'; shulchanaruchharav.com summary

variants.practice: Kiddush and a little food in the sukkah and the meal indoors, or not eating in the sukkah at all; the Baal Shem Tov did not eat in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret.
variants.source: Halachically Speaking vol. 13 no. 17 (citing Meiros Einayim, Otzer Minhagei Chassidim); Kol Torah (R. Jachter, citing Rav Soloveitchik's explanation)

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 668:1; Mishnah Berurah 668:6; Aruch HaShulchan 668:3-5; Korban Netanel 4:7
halacha_index.review_notes: Positions of individual courts (Ger, Belz, Satmar, etc.) were not found. Nitei Gavriel (Four Species pp. 324-344) is the lead for them.
halacha_index.summary_he: השולחן ערוך (או"ח תרסח:א) פוסק שבחוץ לארץ אוכלים בסוכה בשמיני עצרת בלי ברכה. המנהגים בזה מגוונים מאוד.

halacha_index.topic: Hakafot on the night of Shemini Atzeret
halacha_index.summary: Hasidic communities, Chabad included, also hold hakafot on the night of Shemini Atzeret in the diaspora, in addition to Simchat Torah.

variants.practice: Hakafot on Shemini Atzeret night.
variants.source: Chabad.org 'A Deeper Look at Shemini Atzeret / Simchat Torah'

halacha_index.source: Chabad.org, 'A Deeper Look at Shemini Atzeret / Simchat Torah'
halacha_index.review_notes: Single source.
halacha_index.summary_he: קהילות חסידיות, ובהן חב"ד, עורכות בחוץ לארץ הקפות גם בליל שמיני עצרת, נוסף על שמחת תורה.

halacha_index.summary: Each household member lights their own menorah and adds a light each night (mehadrin min ha-mehadrin per the Rema). The candles of each person should be placed apart so the night's number is clear.
common_practices: Each member lights
Blessings precede lighting
halacha_index.source: Rema, Orach Chaim 671:2; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 139:6
halacha_index.review_notes: Practice for wives and daughters varies ('classically the wife did not light', per NHBZ guide); refer to family custom.
halacha_index.summary_he: כל בן בית מדליק מנורה משלו ומוסיף נר בכל לילה (מהדרין מן המהדרין לפי הרמ"א). יש להניח את נרותיו של כל אחד בנפרד, כדי שיהיה ברור מספר הנרות של אותו לילה.

halacha_index.summary: German custom has a documented chapter on reciting She-hecheyanu at the morning Megillah reading.

variants.practice: She-hecheyanu recited at the morning reading.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, chapter 'Reciting She-hecheyanu on Purim Morning', p. 124

halacha_index.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, p. 124 (chapter title)
halacha_index.review_notes: Only the chapter title was seen; the content and details were not read.
halacha_index.summary_he: במנהג גרמניה יש פרק מתועד על אמירת שהחיינו בקריאת המגילה בבוקר.

halacha_index.summary: The custom of Ashkenaz is not to eat kitniyot (rice, legumes, etc.) on Pesach. They are not forbidden if they fall into a dish (batel be-rov), and may be kept in the house and used for benefit such as lamp oil.
common_practices: Kitniyot not eaten
May own kitniyot
Mixtures batel be-rov (Chayei Adam 127; Mishnah Berurah 453:9)
Leniency in famine or illness (Mishnah Berurah 453:7; Aruch HaShulchan 453:5)
halacha_index.source: Rema, Orach Chaim 453:1; Mishnah Berurah 453:7, 453:9; Aruch HaShulchan 453:5
halacha_index.review_notes: Kitniyot oil and the scope of the category (e.g. mustard, per Taz 453:1) are debated; see etzion.org.il 'The Laws of Pesach - Kitniyot'.
halacha_index.summary_he: מנהג אשכנז הוא שלא לאכול קטניות (אורז, קטניות ועוד) בפסח. אין הן אסורות אם נפלו לתבשיל (בטל ברוב), ומותר להשאירן בבית ולהשתמש בהן להנאה, כגון שמן לנר.

halacha_index.summary: Chabad.org states that 'many communities, chassidic ones in particular' avoid gebrokts (matzah that came in contact with water after it was fully baked) on the first seven days of Pesach, and Chabad deliberately eats gebrokts on the eighth day. The custom gained prominence around the end of the 18th century.

variants.practice: No gebrokts for the first seven days; eat gebrokts on the last day (prepared after nightfall).
variants.source: Chabad.org, 'Gebrokts: Wetted Matzah' (Yehuda Shurpin)

variants.practice: No general avoidance is documented.
variants.source: Chabad.org, ibid. (custom described as chiefly Hasidic)

halacha_index.source: Chabad.org, 'Gebrokts: Wetted Matzah'; Shulchan Aruch HaRav OC 460 (cited there)
halacha_index.review_notes: Non-Hasidic Ashkenazim eating gebrokts is the default, but no positive source for it was opened. Belz eighth-day gebrokts is reported only on a forum and is excluded.
halacha_index.summary_he: לפי אתר חב"ד, "קהילות רבות, חסידיות בעיקר" נמנעות מגברוקטס (מצה שבאה במגע עם מים אחרי שנאפתה כולה) בשבעת ימי הפסח הראשונים, וחב"ד אוכלת גברוקטס במכוון ביום השמיני. המנהג תפס מקום בולט בסביבות סוף המאה ה-18.

halacha_index.summary: Chabad does not eat matzah from thirty days before Pesach. On the last day of Pesach it holds Moshiach's Seudah (Moshiach's meal).

variants.practice: No matzah from 30 days before Pesach; Moshiach's Seudah on Acharon shel Pesach.
variants.source: Chabad.org 'Halachot Uminhagim - Laws and Customs of Passover'; Chabad.org 'Eighth Day: Gebrokts and Moshiach's Feast'

halacha_index.source: Chabad.org, 'Halachot Uminhagim — Laws and Customs of Passover'
halacha_index.summary_he: חב"ד אינה אוכלת מצה מתחילת שלושים יום לפני פסח. באחרון של פסח היא עורכת את סעודת משיח.

halacha_index.topic: Hallel in synagogue on the first night
halacha_index.summary: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz documents the recitation of Hallel in the synagogue on the first night of Pesach as a German custom.

variants.practice: Hallel in shul at Maariv on the first night.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, chapter title p. 127

halacha_index.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, p. 127 (chapter title)
halacha_index.review_notes: Chapter title only; it is not established whether German practice is to say it or to omit it. Hasidic Nusach Sefard practice was not sourced.
halacha_index.summary_he: הספר "שורשי מנהג אשכנז" מתעד את אמירת ההלל בבית הכנסת בליל פסח הראשון כמנהג גרמני.

halacha_index.summary: Weddings and haircuts are avoided during part of the Omer. The Rema records two main customs, and must-not-combine-leniencies applies (Rema 493:3).
common_practices: No weddings or haircuts during the chosen 33 days
Lag BaOmer: haircuts, a little rejoicing, no Tachanun (Rema 493:2)
Ba'alei brit (father, sandek, mohel) may cut hair (Rema 493:2; MB 493:12)

variants.practice: From Pesach until Lag BaOmer; haircut on the 33rd day (or Friday if Lag BaOmer is Sunday).
variants.source: Rema OC 493:2 citing Maharil

variants.practice: From Rosh Chodesh Iyar until Shavuot, except Lag BaOmer.
variants.source: Rema OC 493:3; Darkhei Moshe 493:3

variants.practice: From the first day of Rosh Chodesh Iyar until the morning of 3 Sivan.
variants.source: R. Yirmiyohu Kaganoff, 'The Mourning Period of Sefirah'; Mishnah Berurah 493:15

variants.practice: From the day after Pesach until the day before Shavuot, suspended only on Lag BaOmer.
variants.source: Chabad.org 'Mourning Observances of the Sefirat HaOmer Period'

variants.practice: Omer mourning modelled on the twelve months for a parent; shaving permitted; private music permitted, public celebrations not.
variants.source: Nefesh HaRav pp. 191-2, cited by etzion.org.il and Halachipedia

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Aruch and Rema, Orach Chaim 493:1-3; Mishnah Berurah 493:6, 493:15; Aruch HaShulchan 493:4
halacha_index.review_notes: Rav Moshe Feinstein forbids music during the Omer (Igrot Moshe OC 2:137) and allows changing one's set of days year to year (Igrot Moshe OC 1:159), as cited by etzion.org.il and Cong. KINS.

references.title: Mourning and Music in the Omer
Mourning's End - Understanding Sefira and Lag B'Omer - Beyond BT

halacha_index.summary_he: נמנעים מחתונות ומתספורת בחלק מימי העומר. הרמ"א מביא שני מנהגים עיקריים, ואין לערבב קולות משני המנהגים (רמ"א תצג:ג).

halacha_index.topic: Dairy, greenery, night study, and the time of Kiddush
halacha_index.summary: It is customary to eat dairy on the first day, originally as a dairy course followed by meat, with a separate challah. Kiddush is delayed until nightfall so the Omer weeks are 'complete'. The night is spent in Torah study.
common_practices: Dairy then meat (Rema 494:3)
Kiddush after nightfall (Magen Avraham 494:1)
All-night learning (Mishnah Berurah 494:1)

variants.practice: Decorating the shul with greenery.
variants.source: Rema OC 494:2 (as cited in NHBZ Guide to Shavuot 5786)

variants.subgroup: Followers of the Gra; per Aruch HaShulchan and Igrot Moshe
variants.practice: Refrain from greenery.
variants.source: Aruch HaShulchan OC 494:6; Igrot Moshe YD 4:11:5 (as cited ibid.)

variants.practice: Distinct customs on the time of Arvit and Kiddush and on Tikkun Leil Shavuot are documented.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, pp. 134 and 139 (chapter titles)

halacha_index.source: Rema, Orach Chaim 494:2-3; Magen Avraham 494:1, 494:6; Mishnah Berurah 494:1, 494:12
halacha_index.review_notes: Rabbi Dr. Ari Z. Zivotofsky (Jewish Action, 'What's the Truth about... a Dairy Meal on Shavuot?', 2025) labels as a 'misconception' the idea that 'it is a time-honored custom to eat a milchig (dairy) meal on Shavuot'; the original custom was a dairy appetizer before a meat meal.
halacha_index.topic_he: מאכלי חלב, ירק, לימוד בלילה וזמן הקידוש
halacha_index.summary_he: נהוג לאכול מאכלי חלב ביום הראשון, בתחילה כמנה חלבית ואחריה בשרית, עם חלה נפרדת. מאחרים את הקידוש עד צאת הכוכבים, כדי ששבועות העומר יהיו "תמימות". הלילה עובר בלימוד תורה.

halacha_index.summary: The Rema records the custom of waiting one hour after a meat meal and birkat hamazon, but recommends six hours. Ashkenazi subgroups preserve different waiting times.
common_practices: Six hours, which OU Torah (R. Ari Enkin) calls 'the most widespread custom'; 'one whose family's custom is to wait six hours may not change to the three-hour or one-hour custom'
Wait after hard cheese as after meat (Rema YD 89:2)

variants.subgroup: East European Ashkenazim (Litvish, Hasidic, most Modern Orthodox)
variants.practice: Six hours.
variants.source: Rema YD 89:1; Shach 89:8

variants.practice: Three hours.
variants.source: Darchei Teshuvah 89:3 as cited by dinonline.org; OU Torah outorah.org/p/237857

variants.practice: One hour.
variants.source: Rema YD 89:1; OU Torah outorah.org/p/237857

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Aruch and Rema, Yoreh De'ah 89:1
halacha_index.review_notes: OU Torah notes that many German authorities themselves required six hours, and that R. Elyashiv held all in Israel must wait six. A family custom of six should not be changed.
halacha_index.summary_he: הרמ"א מביא את המנהג להמתין שעה אחת אחרי סעודת בשר וברכת המזון, אך ממליץ על שש שעות. עדות המשנה האשכנזיות שומרות על זמני המתנה שונים.

halacha_index.summary: German custom makes a Torah binder (Wimpel) from the cloth used at the brit and later brings it to the synagogue (Schultragen). German custom also has a documented chapter on reciting She-hecheyanu at a brit. The Munkacs custom of a wide sandek's chair is reported by a secondary source.

variants.practice: Wimpel from the brit cloth; Schultragen; She-hecheyanu at the brit.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, chapters pp. 179, 191, 206

variants.practice: A very wide chair so it appears as two seats, one for Eliyahu and one for the sandek.
variants.source: Darkei Chaim VeShalom 519, as cited by shulchanaruchharav.com 'Where the Sandek should sit'

halacha_index.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis (2010), table of contents
halacha_index.review_notes: Munkacs item is second-hand (not opened in Darkei Chaim VeShalom itself).
halacha_index.summary_he: במנהג גרמניה עושים וימפל (חגורת ספר תורה) מהבד ששימש בברית, ומביאים אותו מאוחר יותר לבית הכנסת (שולטראגן). במנהג גרמניה יש גם פרק מתועד על אמירת שהחיינו בברית. מנהג מונקאטש של כיסא רחב לסנדק מובא ממקור משני.

halacha_index.summary: Many Hasidic communities leave a boy's hair uncut until his third Hebrew birthday and then hold an upsherin, leaving the peyot. The custom stems from the Ari's circle in Safed and Meron. It was never part of Minhag Ashkenaz.

variants.practice: At the third Hebrew birthday; the boy then begins wearing kippah and tzitzit.
variants.source: Chabad.org 'The Basics of the Upsherin'; Chabad.org 'The Upsherin'

variants.practice: At age two.
variants.source: Mishpacha Magazine 'Upsheren' (Skver); shulchanaruchharav.com 'When to perform the Upsherinish', footnote citing Peulas Tzadik 3:236 (Gur, Skver)

variants.practice: No chalaka; hair cut when needed, already within the first months.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz vol. 3 pp. 251-267, chapter 'Cutting A Boy's Hair Without Doing a Chalaka'

variants.practice: Opposed the Meron chalaka.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz, ibid.

halacha_index.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz, 'Cutting A Boy's Hair Without Doing a Chalaka (Upsherin)', pp. 212ff of the synopsis
halacha_index.review_notes: The Ger age-two custom rests on secondary sources; Peulas Tzadik was not opened.

references.title: The Basics of the Upsherin - A Boy's First Haircut - Chabad.org

halacha_index.summary_he: קהילות חסידיות רבות מניחות לשערו של הילד לגדול עד יום הולדתו השלישי העברי, ואז עורכות אופשערן ומשאירות את הפאות. המנהג נובע מחוגו של האר"י בצפת ובמירון. הוא מעולם לא היה חלק ממנהג אשכנז.

halacha_index.summary: The chatan and kallah fast on the day of their chuppah, reciting Aneinu at Mincha, as on a personal Yom Kippur. The chuppah is held under the open sky as a blessing that their descendants be as the stars. Weddings are preferably scheduled early in the month.
common_practices: Fast until the chuppah
Al Chet / viduy at Mincha
Outdoor chuppah (Rema EH 61:1)
Wedding early in the month (Rema EH 64:3; SA YD 179:2)

variants.practice: The father of the bride also fasts.
variants.source: Institute for Jewish Ideas and Ideals, 'Comparative Study of the Sephardic and Ashkenazic Wedding Ceremony'

variants.practice: Chuppat tallit (tallit spread over bride and groom), throwing wheat on the couple, two chuppot on the wedding day, Mahnführen, singing for the groom in shul.
variants.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, chapters pp. 143-173; R. Yaakov Kamenetsky endorsing chuppat tallit (Introduction p. 12)

halacha_index.source: Rema, Even HaEzer 61:1 and Orach Chaim 573:1; Sefer HaRokeach 353; Maharam Mintz 109
halacha_index.review_notes: The fast is not held on days when fasting is forbidden, such as Rosh Chodesh; see Eretz Hemdah Ask the Rabbi vol. III.

references.title: Comparative Study of the Sephardic and Ashkenazic Wedding Ceremony

halacha_index.summary_he: החתן והכלה צמים ביום חופתם ואומרים "עננו" במנחה, כמו ביום כיפור אישי. החופה נערכת תחת כיפת השמיים, כברכה שצאצאיהם יהיו ככוכבים. עדיף לקבוע חתונות בתחילת החודש.

halacha_index.summary: Former Satmar women describe a communal requirement for married women to shave their heads.

variants.practice: Head shaved after marriage, as reported in memoir accounts.
variants.source: The Forward, 'Ex-Hasidic Woman Marks Five Years Since She Shaved Her Head'; Frieda Vizel podcast #32

halacha_index.source: Forward (first-person essay); friedavizel.com podcast #32
halacha_index.review_notes: Only anecdotal accounts by former members; no Satmar halachic source found. Claims about Belz are unreliable and are excluded. Do not display without review.
halacha_index.summary_he: נשים שעזבו את סאטמר מתארות דרישה קהילתית שנשים נשואות יגלחו את ראשן.

halacha_index.summary: On a parent's yahrzeit the child recites Kaddish. Fasting is described by the Rema as a mitzvah. The child avoids weddings and similar music celebrations.
common_practices: Kaddish on the yahrzeit day itself (not the preceding Shabbat)
Avoid weddings and sheva berachot on the yahrzeit (Darkhei Moshe YD 391:3; Shach and Taz agree for every year)
Fast not observed on Rosh Chodesh (Chochmat Adam 171:11)

variants.practice: Kaddish only on the yahrzeit day.
variants.source: shulchanaruchharav.com 'Chapter 28: The Yartzite', citing Rema YD 376:4

variants.practice: Fasting on the yahrzeit is no longer common.
variants.source: shulchanaruchharav.com, ibid.; Chabad.org 'Yahrzeit Prayers'

halacha_index.source: Rema, Yoreh De'ah 376:4 (Kaddish, citing Maharil); Rema YD 376:4/402:12 (fast); Darkhei Moshe YD 391:3
halacha_index.review_notes: Sources number the fast passage differently (Kaganoff: 376:5 and 402:12); verify the seif. Sources differ on whether fasting is still the practice.
halacha_index.summary_he: ביום היארצייט של הורה הילד אומר קדיש. הרמ"א מתאר את הצום כמצווה. הילד נמנע מחתונות ומשמחות דומות שיש בהן מוזיקה.

halacha_index.summary: Many Hasidic communities refrain from Torah study on Christmas eve (Nittel). Munkacs sources also limit marital relations that night, with leniency after midnight on a mikveh night.

variants.practice: No Torah study on Nittel; marital relations avoided (lenient after midnight on mikveh night).
variants.source: Darkei Chaim VeShalom 825, 828, as cited by shulchanaruchharav.com 'Custom of Nittle Nacht'

halacha_index.source: Darkei Chaim VeShalom 825, 828 (as cited by a secondary source)
halacha_index.review_notes: Second-hand section numbers only; other courts' practice (e.g. Chabad) not sourced here.
halacha_index.summary_he: קהילות חסידיות רבות נמנעות מלימוד תורה בערב חג המולד (ניטל). מקורות מונקאטש מגבילים גם תשמיש המיטה באותו לילה, ומקלים אחרי חצות בליל טבילה.

halacha_index.summary: Munkacs sources say one begins wishing 'Leshana Tova' from the 15th of Av.

variants.practice: Leshana Tova greetings from Tu B'Av.
variants.source: Darkei Chaim VeShalom 684 and Shaar Yisachar, as cited by shulchanaruchharav.com 'Customs of Elul'

halacha_index.source: Darkei Chaim VeShalom 684 (as cited by a secondary source)
halacha_index.review_notes: Single secondary source.
halacha_index.summary_he: מקורות מונקאטש אומרים שמתחילים לאחל "לשנה טובה" מט"ו באב.

unique_minhagim.name: Wimpel and Schultragen
unique_minhagim.description: A Torah binder sewn from the cloth used at a boy's brit, later brought by the child to the synagogue (Schultragen) and used to wrap the Sefer Torah.
unique_minhagim.when: Brit, then the child's first visit to shul
unique_minhagim.description_he: חגורת ספר תורה התפורה מהבד ששימש בברית של בן, שהילד מביא אותה מאוחר יותר לבית הכנסת (שולטראגן) והיא משמשת לעטיפת ספר התורה.

unique_minhagim.name: Breslov Rosh Hashana kibbutz
unique_minhagim.description: Gathering of Breslov Hasidim at R. Nachman's grave in Uman, organized by R. Nosson from 1811.
unique_minhagim.description_he: התכנסות של חסידי ברסלב על קבר רבי נחמן באומן, שרבי נתן ארגן מאז 1811.

unique_minhagim.name: Moshiach's Seudah
unique_minhagim.description: Festive meal on the last day of Pesach focused on the future redemption, with gebrokts eaten deliberately.
unique_minhagim.source: Chabad.org, 'Eighth Day: Gebrokts and Moshiach's Feast'
unique_minhagim.description_he: סעודה חגיגית באחרון של פסח, המוקדשת לגאולה העתידה, שבה אוכלים גברוקטס במכוון.

unique_minhagim.name: Upsherin
unique_minhagim.description: First haircut ceremony leaving the peyot, at age three (age two in Ger and Skver); not practiced in Minhag Ashkenaz.
unique_minhagim.source: Chabad.org 'The Basics of the Upsherin'; Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz vol. 3 pp. 251-267
unique_minhagim.description_he: טקס התספורת הראשונה שבו משאירים את הפאות, בגיל שלוש (בגיל שנתיים בגור ובסקווירא). אינו נהוג במנהג אשכנז.

unique_minhagim.name: Chuppat tallit
unique_minhagim.description: Spreading a tallit over the bride and groom under the chuppah, a German custom R. Yaakov Kamenetsky called 'definitely proper to follow'.
unique_minhagim.source: Shorshei Minhag Ashkenaz synopsis, Introduction p. 12 and chapter p. 167
unique_minhagim.description_he: פריסת טלית מעל החתן והכלה תחת החופה, מנהג גרמני שרבי יעקב קמניצקי כינה "ראוי בהחלט ללכת אחריו".

disputes: Tefillin on Chol HaMoed: Shulchan Aruch forbids; Rema wears with beracha; Taz without beracha; Gra, Hasidim and all of Eretz Yisrael do not wear.

Omer mourning dates: Pesach to Lag BaOmer vs Rosh Chodesh Iyar to Shavuot vs Rosh Chodesh Iyar to 3 Sivan vs entire Omer except Lag BaOmer (Chabad); Soloveitchik permits shaving and private music, Igrot Moshe forbids music.
Sukkah on Shemini Atzeret: Shulchan Aruch and Chabad eat everything in the sukkah; many Hasidim make Kiddush only or do not eat there.
Meat-to-dairy wait: six hours (Rema's recommendation, majority) vs three (German) vs one (Dutch, Rema's base custom).
Shavuot greenery: Rema endorses; Aruch HaShulchan and Igrot Moshe report refraining (Gra).
Yahrzeit fast: Rema calls it a mitzvah; contemporary sources say it is no longer customary.
Upsherin: age three (Chabad, most Hasidim) vs age two (Ger, Skver) vs not practiced (Minhag Ashkenaz, Chatam Sofer opposed the Meron chalaka).

Exact seif numbering of the Rema on yahrzeit fasting (YD 376:4 vs 376:5 and 402:12)
Chabad hakafot on Shemini Atzeret night (single source)
